Metafiction. Metafiction is fiction that reflexively examines its own nature as constructed narrative, exposing the artifices of storytelling rather than concealing them. A metafictional work might break the fourth wall, reveal its narrator as unreliable or invented, comment on its own plot, or foreground the process of writing itself. This technique emerged as a conscious literary strategy in the twentieth century, particularly among modernist and postmodernist writers who were skeptical of the novel's capacity to represent reality transparently or objectively.

Metafiction rejects the realist contract where the reader suspends disbelief in exchange for the illusion of a real world represented faithfully. Jorge Luis Borges is often credited with inventing metafiction as a major literary mode through stories like The Library of Babel and Tlön, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius. Stories may feature characters who are also writers, novels within novels, or the text acknowledging moments when its own plot becomes confused or contradictory. Metafictional techniques include footnotes that claim questionable authenticity, unreliable narrators who admit they are inventing, and stories that collapse the distinction between reality and fiction.

Flann O'Brien's At Swim-Two-Birds features an author writing a novel within a novel, with his characters rebelling against the author's authority over their fates. Metafiction challenges the reader. It demands active interpretation and acknowledgment that all narratives are constructed, not discovered. The technique intensified in postmodernism but has roots in earlier self-conscious literature like Laurence Sterne's Tristram Shandy. Metafictional works often expose narrative conventions through parody or direct commentary, forcing readers to recognize how stories rely on arbitrary rules and reader cooperation.

Jorge Luis Borges is an Argentine master of metafiction whose stories are foundational to the form's modern development. At Swim-Two-Birds is an Irish novel that features layered narrative, characters who contest their author's control, and comedy derived from narrative instability. Stream of consciousness is a related technique of interior representation that reveals the fragmentary nature of consciousness and language. Postmodernism became a defining practice in which metafiction thrived, embracing artificiality and formal self-awareness. Modernist writers like Joyce and Woolf pioneered some metafictional techniques through narrative innovation.
